Correct: *Rina went to the market yesterday and bought fresh vegetables for the week.*

**Neither** the old table nor the broken chairs **is** fit **to be** used **in** the new office.

Correct: *Neither the old table nor the broken chairs are fit to be used in the new office.*
solution.rule: Subject–verb agreement: neither … nor → the verb agrees with the nearer subject
solution.trap: 'Neither' (bold part 1) suggests a singular verb, and 'table' is singular; the noun next to the verb decides.

The **jewellery** that she **wore** at the wedding **were** **gifted** by her grandmother.

steps: Bold part 3 ('were') is wrong. 'Jewellery' is an uncountable noun and takes a singular verb: 'was gifted'.
Correct: *The jewellery that she wore at the wedding was gifted by her grandmother.*
solution.rule: Subject–verb agreement: uncountable nouns (jewellery, furniture, equipment) take a singular verb
solution.trap: Jewellery usually means several pieces, so a plural verb feels natural; grammatically the noun is singular.

Ajay **did not knew** the **way** to the new branch, **so** he **asked** a shopkeeper.

Correct: *Ajay did not know the way to the new branch, so he asked a shopkeeper.*
solution.rule: Verb form: do / does / did + base verb
solution.trap: The story is in the past, so 'knew' seems to fit; 'did' already carries the past tense.
solution.shortcut: did + V1, never did + V2.

Correct: *The doctor advised him to give up smoking and start walking daily.*
solution.rule: Verb form: start / begin + -ing or to-infinitive
solution.trap: 'to give up … and start' is a correct parallel pair (to give up … and [to] start); the error is the bare 'walk' after 'start'.
solution.shortcut: start / stop / keep / give up + -ing.

There **is** **heavy** traffic **on** the highway ever since the bridge **was closed** for repairs.

steps: Bold part 1 ('is') is wrong. 'Ever since' marks a situation that began in the past and continues now, so the main clause needs the present perfect: 'There has been heavy traffic'.
Correct: *There has been heavy traffic on the highway ever since the bridge was closed for repairs.*
solution.rule: Tense: (ever) since + past point → present perfect in the main clause
solution.trap: 'was closed' (bold part 4) is correct, because the closing was a single past event. The tense to change is in the main clause.
solution.shortcut: Main clause with since → have / has (been).

The candidate **who** applied last week **was** found **ineligible** **of** the post.

Correct: *The candidate who applied last week was found ineligible for the post.*

solution.trap: 'ineligible' (bold part 3) may look like the odd word, but it is correct; only the preposition is wrong.

In the sentence below, four parts are given in bold. Which bold part contains an error? If all are correct, choose 'All are correct'.

**Seldom** **does** the branch manager **leaves** his cabin **before** 7 p.m.

Correct: *Seldom does the branch manager leave his cabin before 7 p.m.*
solution.rule: Inversion: negative adverb (seldom, rarely, never) + does / did + subject + base verb
solution.trap: 'does' (bold part 2) is correct and required by the inversion. With the -s already on 'does', 'leaves' marks the tense a second time.

items.prompt:
In the sentence below, four parts are given in bold. Which bold part contains an error? If all are correct, choose 'All are correct'.

The award **was shared** between Raju and **myself**, **since** we **had worked** on the project together.

steps: Bold part 2 ('myself') is wrong. A reflexive pronoun is used only when it refers back to the subject of the same clause; here the subject is 'the award'. After 'between' the object form is needed: 'between Raju and me'.
Correct: *The award was shared between Raju and me, since we had worked on the project together.*
solution.rule: Pronouns: no reflexive without an antecedent; object form after a preposition
solution.trap: 'myself' sounds modest and formal, which is why it replaces 'me' in speech; 'had worked' is correct, since the work came before the award.
solution.shortcut: Remove 'Raju and': 'shared between myself' is wrong → me.

items.prompt:
In the sentence below, four parts are given in bold. Which bold part contains an error? If all are correct, choose 'All are correct'.

If I **had known** that the branch **was** closed, I **would not have** **wasted** my morning.

steps: All four bold parts are correct. It is a third conditional: if + past perfect ('had known'), would not have + past participle ('wasted'). 'was closed' is the normal past tense in the reported fact.
Correct: *If I had known that the branch was closed, I would not have wasted my morning.*
solution.rule: No error: third conditional — if + had + V3, would (not) have + V3
solution.trap: Some expect 'had been closed' instead of 'was', but the branch was closed at the time of knowing, so the simple past is correct.
solution.shortcut: Check the two halves: had + V3 / would have + V3 → correct.

items.prompt:
In the sentence below, four parts are given in bold. Which bold part contains an error? If all are correct, choose 'All are correct'.

The police **arrived** **quickly**, but **by then** the thieves **escaped**.

steps: Bold part 4 ('escaped') is wrong. 'By then' refers to a point in the past (when the police arrived); an action finished before that point needs the past perfect: 'had escaped'.
Correct: *The police arrived quickly, but by then the thieves had escaped.*
solution.rule: Tense: by then / by the time + past → past perfect for the earlier action
solution.trap: 'arrived' is correct simple past. The two past verbs look consistent, but 'by then' requires the earlier action to be in the past perfect.
solution.shortcut: by then / by that time (past) → had + V3.

items.prompt:
In the sentence below, four parts are given in bold. Which bold part contains an error? If all are correct, choose 'All are correct'.

**Supposing if** the loan **is** rejected, **what** will you **do**?

steps: Bold part 1 ('Supposing if') is wrong. 'Supposing' already means 'if', so 'if' is redundant: 'Supposing the loan is rejected, what will you do?'
Correct: *Supposing the loan is rejected, what will you do?*
solution.rule: Redundancy: supposing / suppose / provided / in case are not followed by 'if'
solution.trap: 'is rejected' with 'will you do' is a correct first conditional, so the rest of the sentence seems fine.
solution.shortcut: Use 'Supposing …' or 'If …', never both.

items.prompt:
In the sentence below, four parts are given in bold. Which bold part contains an error? If all are correct, choose 'All are correct'.

Ravi **told** me that he **has** **met** the manager the **previous** day.

steps: Bold part 2 ('has') is wrong. In reported speech after a past reporting verb, 'met' (or 'have met') moves back to the past perfect: 'he had met the manager the previous day'. A present perfect also cannot go with a definite past time such as 'the previous day'.
Correct: *Ravi told me that he had met the manager the previous day.*
solution.rule: Reported speech: past reporting verb → backshift (past / present perfect → past perfect)
solution.trap: 'previous' (bold part 4) is the correct reported form of 'yesterday'; it is a clue that the verb must also be shifted.
solution.shortcut: told + 'the previous day' → had + V3.

items.prompt:
In the sentence below, four parts are given in bold. Which bold part contains an error? If all are correct, choose 'All are correct'.

**Owing to** his **illness**, Rajesh **could not** **attend to** the board meeting.

steps: Bold part 4 ('attend to') is wrong. 'Attend a meeting' (be present at) takes no preposition; 'attend to' means 'deal with' or 'look after' (attend to a customer). It should be 'attend the board meeting'.
Correct: *Owing to his illness, Rajesh could not attend the board meeting.*
solution.rule: Prepositions: attend (a meeting / class) — no preposition; attend to = deal with
solution.trap: 'attend to' is a real phrasal verb, so it looks correct; its meaning does not fit 'the board meeting'. 'Owing to' is correct here.
solution.shortcut: attend a meeting; attend to a problem / a patient.

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: My brother and his friend goes to the gym near our colony every morning before work.
The bank remains closed on the second and fourth Saturdays of every month.
Please keep your passbook ready so that the clerk can update it quickly at the counter.
Our neighbour has been teaching mathematics at the government school for nearly twelve years.

steps: Sentence A is incorrect. Two subjects joined by 'and' ('my brother and his friend') make a plural subject, so the verb must be 'go', not 'goes'.
Correct: *My brother and his friend go to the gym near our colony every morning before work.*
The other three are correct: B has the singular subject 'bank' with 'remains'; C has the base verb 'update' after the modal 'can'; D uses the present perfect continuous with 'for' + a period.
solution.rule: Subject–verb agreement: X and Y → plural verb
solution.trap: 'his friend', a singular noun, sits right before the verb and pulls you towards 'goes'.
solution.shortcut: Replace the subject with 'they': they go.

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: The new canteen in our office serves hot idlis and filter coffee every morning.
My grandmother tells us interesting stories about her childhood in a small village near Madurai.
The police collected several evidences from the house where the theft took place.
Ravi forgot his umbrella at home, so he got completely wet in the rain.

steps: Sentence C is incorrect. 'Evidence' is an uncountable noun: it has no plural and cannot follow 'several'. Use 'several pieces of evidence' or 'a lot of evidence'.
Correct: *The police collected several pieces of evidence from the house where the theft took place.*
The other three are correct: A has the singular 'canteen' with 'serves'; B is a simple present habit with a singular subject; D has both clauses in the simple past, joined by 'so'.
solution.rule: Countability: 'evidence' is uncountable
solution.trap: 'The police collected' is correct ('police' is plural); the error is the plural 'evidences'.
solution.shortcut: evidence, advice, information, equipment → no -s.

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: Every Sunday, my father cleans his scooter and checks the air in the tyres.
The students were excited because the school had announced a trip to Mysuru Palace.
If you need any help with the form, please ask the lady at the enquiry desk.
Last week, Meera has bought a new mobile phone with the money she had saved.

steps: Sentence D is incorrect. 'Last week' is a finished past time, so the present perfect 'has bought' is wrong; the simple past 'bought' is needed.
Correct: *Last week, Meera bought a new mobile phone with the money she had saved.*
The other three are correct: A uses the simple present for a routine; B uses the past perfect for the earlier action (the announcement); C is a correct real conditional with an imperative.
solution.rule: Tense: simple past with a definite past time (last week, yesterday, in 2020)
solution.trap: 'had saved' may look odd, but the saving came before the buying, so the past perfect there is correct.
solution.shortcut: Finished time word → simple past.

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: The parking area behind the branch is reserved for staff vehicles on working days.
One of the cashiers in our branch have been selected for a training programme in Mumbai.
Neha and her colleagues ordered lunch from a nearby restaurant to celebrate her promotion.
The auditor checked every voucher carefully before signing the final report of the branch.

steps: Sentence B is incorrect. The subject is 'one' (of the cashiers), which is singular, so the verb must be 'has been selected'.
Correct: *One of the cashiers in our branch has been selected for a training programme in Mumbai.*

The other three are correct: A agrees 'is' with the singular 'parking area'; C has a compound subject with a past verb, so there is no agreement issue; D uses 'every' with a singular noun and a gerund after 'before'.
solution.rule: Subject–verb agreement: 'one of the + plural noun' → singular verb
solution.trap: The plural 'cashiers' and 'branch' stand between 'one' and the verb.
solution.shortcut: Cover 'of the cashiers in our branch': 'One … has been selected'.

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: The manager thanked the security guard for his presence of mind during the robbery attempt.
Anjali felt proud when her parents came to watch her receive the best employee award.
The children promised their teacher that they would finish the project by Friday.
The bank sent letters of appreciation to my colleague and I for completing the audit early.

steps: Sentence D is incorrect. 'my colleague and I' is the object of the preposition 'to', so the object pronoun is needed: 'to my colleague and me'.
Correct: *The bank sent letters of appreciation to my colleague and me for completing the audit early.*
The other three are correct: A uses the idiom 'presence of mind' correctly; B has a bare infinitive ('receive') after 'watch her'; C backshifts 'will' to 'would' after the past verb 'promised'.
solution.rule: Pronoun case: object form after a preposition
solution.trap: '… and I' is often taught as the polite form, but it is right only in subject position.
solution.shortcut: Drop 'my colleague and': 'sent letters to I' is clearly wrong.

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: Mr Iyer is working as a branch manager in Coimbatore since the beginning of 2022.
The old post office building was converted into a museum after it was renovated.
We reached the railway station just in time to catch the last train to Lucknow.
The villagers have planted more than five hundred saplings along the canal this year.

steps: Sentence A is incorrect. An action that began in the past ('since the beginning of 2022') and continues now needs the present perfect continuous: 'has been working'.
Correct: *Mr Iyer has been working as a branch manager in Coimbatore since the beginning of 2022.*
The other three are correct: B is a correct passive in the simple past; C uses 'just in time to' + verb correctly; D uses the present perfect with 'this year', a period not yet over.
solution.rule: Tense: 'since' + point of time → present perfect (continuous)
solution.trap: The sentence describes his present job, so the present continuous feels right; 'since' makes the present perfect necessary.
solution.shortcut: since / for up to now → has been + -ing.

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: You should switch off the lights and fans before leaving the office in the evening.
The clerk asked me to return back the old debit card when I collected the new one.
The customer was asked to visit the branch with a copy of her PAN card.
Students who want to apply for the scholarship must submit their forms by Monday.

steps: Sentence B is incorrect. 'Return' already means 'give back' or 'go back', so 'return back' is redundant. Use 'return the old debit card'.
Correct: *The clerk asked me to return the old debit card when I collected the new one.*
The other three are correct: A has 'should' + base verb and a gerund after 'before'; C is a correct passive with a to-infinitive; D has 'must' + base verb and a plural relative clause.
solution.rule: Redundancy: return back, repeat again, revert back → drop 'back' / 'again'
solution.trap: 'return back' is common in Indian speech, so it sounds normal; the meaning of 'back' is already in 'return'.
solution.shortcut: re- words (return, repeat, revert) need no 'back' or 'again'.

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: There is very few water left in the tank, so we must use it carefully.
The patient was too weak to walk, so the nurse helped him into the wheelchair.
My aunt runs a small tailoring shop and employs four women from the neighbourhood.
The tea stall outside the station opens at five in the morning for early commuters.

steps: Sentence A is incorrect. 'Water' is uncountable, so it takes 'little', not 'few': 'very little water'.
Correct: *There is very little water left in the tank, so we must use it carefully.*
The other three are correct: B uses 'too … to' correctly; C keeps both verbs in the simple present with a singular subject; D has the singular 'tea stall' with 'opens'.
solution.rule: Countability: little + uncountable; few + countable plural
solution.trap: 'There is' is correct (water is singular), which makes the sentence look fine at first glance.
solution.shortcut: Countable? No → little / much / less.

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: Mumbai's local trains are often crowded during the morning and evening rush hours.
Our new branch is much bigger than the old one and has a separate counter for pensioners.
This is the most comfortable bus I have ever travelled in on this route.
Among all the trainees in the batch, Arjun is the more hardworking and sincere.

steps: Sentence D is incorrect. 'Among all the trainees' compares Arjun with more than two people, so the superlative is needed: 'the most hardworking and sincere'.
Correct: *Among all the trainees in the batch, Arjun is the most hardworking and sincere.*
The other three are correct: A has the plural subject 'trains' with 'are'; B uses 'much' to strengthen a comparative ('much bigger'); C has a superlative followed by 'I have ever …'.
solution.rule: Degrees of comparison: superlative for three or more; comparative only for two
solution.trap: 'the more …' is right with 'Of the two'; here 'all the trainees' is a larger group.
solution.shortcut: Group of more than two → most / -est.

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: The new clerk is not well acquainted about the rules for opening joint accounts.
My sister is fond of reading detective novels during her long train journeys.
The farmer was confident of getting a good price for his cotton this season.
We congratulated our colleague on his promotion to the post of assistant manager.

steps: Sentence A is incorrect. 'Acquainted' takes the preposition 'with': 'acquainted with the rules'.
Correct: *The new clerk is not well acquainted with the rules for opening joint accounts.*
The other three are correct: B uses 'fond of' + gerund; C uses 'confident of' + gerund; D uses 'congratulate someone on'.
solution.rule: Prepositions: acquainted with, familiar with, aware of
solution.trap: 'aware of' and 'know about' are close in meaning, which leads to 'acquainted about'.

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: Although the queue was long, the clerk at the counter served everyone with a smile.
The shop was closed when we arrived, so we decided to come back the next day.
Neither the manager or his deputy was available when the customer called the branch.
Unless you fill in every column of the form, the bank cannot process your request.

steps: Sentence C is incorrect. 'Neither' pairs with 'nor', not 'or': 'Neither the manager nor his deputy was available'.
Correct: *Neither the manager nor his deputy was available when the customer called the branch.*
The other three are correct: A uses 'although' with no extra 'but'; B joins two past clauses with 'so'; D uses 'unless' without a second negative in its clause.
solution.rule: Correlative conjunctions: neither … nor; either … or
solution.trap: 'was' is correct here (the nearer subject 'deputy' is singular), so the verb is not the problem.
solution.shortcut: neither ↔ nor, either ↔ or: never mix them.

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: Our office used to close at six, but now it closes at half past five.
Many residents objected to cut down the old trees for widening the road.
The children were told to wash their hands before eating their mid-day meal.
My parents have decided to spend the summer holidays with our relatives in Shillong.

steps: Sentence B is incorrect. In 'object to', 'to' is a preposition and must be followed by a gerund: 'objected to cutting down the old trees'.
Correct: *Many residents objected to cutting down the old trees for widening the road.*
The other three are correct: A uses 'used to' + base verb for a past habit; C has a gerund after the preposition 'before'; D uses 'decide' + to-infinitive.
solution.rule: Verb form: object to / look forward to / be used to + -ing
solution.trap: 'to cut' looks like a normal infinitive; test with a noun: 'objected to the plan' works, so 'to' is a preposition.
solution.shortcut: Noun fits after 'to'? → -ing.

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: The team of doctors examined the patients at the camp and distributed free medicines.
Every passenger on the bus was asked to show a valid ticket to the inspector.
The cattle were moved to higher ground before the river began to overflow.
Each of the new accounts opened this month need to be verified by the manager.

steps: Sentence D is incorrect. 'Each' is the subject and is singular, so the verb must be 'needs'.
Correct: *Each of the new accounts opened this month needs to be verified by the manager.*
The other three are correct: A uses past verbs, so there is no agreement problem with 'team'; B has 'every' + singular noun + singular verb; C treats 'cattle' as plural, which it always is.
solution.rule: Subject–verb agreement: each of + plural noun → singular verb
solution.trap: 'accounts' and 'month' come between 'each' and the verb; 'month' is singular too, which hides the mistake.
solution.shortcut: Each … needs / has / is.

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: The clerk told me that the cheque book will be delivered to my address the following week.
The manager asked whether I had brought the original documents for verification.
Seema said that she was feeling tired after the long journey from Guwahati.
The teacher reminded the students that the exam would begin at ten sharp.

steps: Sentence A is incorrect. The statement is reported with a past verb ('told') and 'the following week', so 'will' must shift back to 'would': 'would be delivered'.
Correct: *The clerk told me that the cheque book would be delivered to my address the following week.*

The other three are correct: B uses statement order and the past perfect in a reported question; C backshifts 'am feeling' to 'was feeling'; D backshifts 'will' to 'would' after a past reporting verb.
solution.rule: Reported speech: past reporting verb → will becomes would
solution.trap: 'the following week' is already the reported form of 'next week', and it confirms that the verb must shift as well.
solution.shortcut: told / said + 'the following week' → would.

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: The office has bought new chairs and tables for the waiting area near the cash counter.
The office assistant ordered fresh stationeries such as registers, pens and files for the branch.
A few customers complained that the ATM had run out of cash on Sunday.
The children planted vegetables in the school garden as part of their science project.

steps: Sentence B is incorrect. 'Stationery' (writing materials) is an uncountable noun and has no plural. It should be 'fresh stationery'.
Correct: *The office assistant ordered fresh stationery such as registers, pens and files for the branch.*
The other three are correct: A uses countable plurals ('chairs and tables') correctly; C has 'a few' + countable plural; D is a simple past sentence with a plural subject.
solution.rule: Countability: 'stationery' is uncountable
solution.trap: The list 'registers, pens and files' is plural, which makes a plural noun feel natural.
solution.shortcut: stationery, machinery, jewellery, crockery → no -s.

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: The festival lights made the whole street look bright and colourful at night.
The soup at this dhaba tastes delicious, especially on a cold winter evening.
The cashier counted the notes very careful before handing them over to the customer.
The bus driver drove slowly through the crowded market to avoid an accident.

steps: Sentence C is incorrect. 'Careful' describes how the cashier counted, which is an action, so the adverb is needed: 'very carefully'.
Correct: *The cashier counted the notes very carefully before handing them over to the customer.*
The other three are correct: A has adjectives after the linking verb 'look'; B has an adjective after the linking verb 'tastes'; D uses the adverb 'slowly' with the action verb 'drove'.
solution.rule: Adjective vs adverb: action verb + adverb; linking verb + adjective
solution.trap: Sentences A and B also have an adjective after the verb and are correct, because 'look' and 'taste' are linking verbs there. 'Count' is an action verb.
solution.shortcut: Ask 'how did he count?' → -ly.

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: The bank has warned its customers against sharing their passwords with strangers.
My cousin is good at drawing and wants to become an architect.
The security guard prevented the stray dogs from entering the hospital premises at night.
The villagers are complaining for the irregular supply of electricity in their area.

steps: Sentence D is incorrect. 'Complain' takes 'about' (or 'of'), not 'for': 'complaining about the irregular supply of electricity'.
Correct: *The villagers are complaining about the irregular supply of electricity in their area.*
The other three are correct: A uses 'warn against' + gerund; B uses 'good at' + gerund; C uses 'prevent … from' + gerund.
solution.rule: Prepositions: complain about / of (something), complain to (someone)
solution.trap: 'for' follows 'ask' and 'demand' in Indian speech ('ask for a better supply'), so 'complain for' sounds possible.

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: My cousin brother is coming from Bhopal to attend my sister's wedding next month.
Please return the file to the record room after you have finished checking it.
The meeting was postponed because the chairman was stuck in heavy traffic.
An honest officer never accepts gifts from customers whose loans he has sanctioned.

steps: Sentence A is incorrect. 'Cousin brother' is redundant in standard English; 'cousin' already covers the relationship. Write 'My cousin' (or 'My cousin, Arvind,' with a name).
Correct: *My cousin is coming from Bhopal to attend my sister's wedding next month.*
The other three are correct: B uses the present perfect in a time clause; C is a correct passive with a reason clause; D uses 'an' before the silent 'h' in 'honest' and 'whose' correctly.
solution.rule: Redundancy: cousin brother / cousin sister → cousin
solution.trap: The phrase is everyday Indian English, so it does not feel like an error; exams treat it as redundant.

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: The spectacles that my grandfather wears for reading have a thick black frame.
Either the clerk or the peons have to open the branch at nine every morning.
Two hours is enough time to finish the audit of this small branch.
The bank's new branch, along with its ATM, was inaugurated by the district collector.

steps: All four sentences are correct. Each one uses a pattern that looks wrong at first but is standard.

A: 'spectacles' is plural-only, so 'have' is right; B: with 'either … or' the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'peons' → 'have'; C: a period of time taken as one amount takes 'is'; D: 'along with its ATM' does not change the singular subject 'branch' → 'was'.
solution.rule: No error: plural-only nouns, either … or proximity, amounts as a unit, 'along with'
solution.trap: Each sentence has a trap that suggests an error (spectacles … have, clerk … have, hours … is, ATM … was). Check each against its rule before marking it.
solution.shortcut: Mark a sentence only when you can name the rule it breaks.

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: A number of senior citizens were waiting outside the branch before it opened.
The number of customers using mobile banking in rural areas have grown rapidly since the pandemic.
Neither the cashier nor the clerks were aware that the vault key was missing.
The committee has finally approved the proposal to set up a new ATM near the bus stand.

steps: Sentence B is incorrect. 'The number of …' takes a singular verb, because the subject is 'the number'. It should be 'has grown'.
Correct: *The number of customers using mobile banking in rural areas has grown rapidly since the pandemic.*
The other three are correct: A 'a number of' (= many) takes a plural verb; C the verb agrees with the nearer subject 'clerks' → 'were'; D the committee acts as one body → 'has'.
solution.rule: Subject–verb agreement: the number of → singular; a number of → plural
solution.trap: Sentence A ('A number of … were') is correct and looks like the same pattern; the article decides: 'a number' = many, 'the number' = a figure.
solution.shortcut: the number … has; a number of … have.

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: By the time the auditors arrived, the clerk had already prepared all the registers.
She has been teaching at this college ever since she moved to Dehradun in 2015.
If it rains heavily tonight, the match will be shifted to the indoor stadium.
I wish I have more time to prepare for the mains examination this year.

steps: Sentence D is incorrect. A wish about the present is expressed with the past simple: 'I wish I had more time'. The present tense 'have' cannot follow 'wish'.
Correct: *I wish I had more time to prepare for the mains examination this year.*

The other three are correct: A uses the past perfect for the action finished before 'arrived'; B uses the present perfect continuous in the main clause and the simple past after 'since'; C is a first conditional with the simple present in the if-clause.
solution.rule: Wish: wish + past simple for a present situation; wish + past perfect for a past one
solution.trap: 'this year' points to the present, which makes 'have' feel right; 'wish' always moves the verb one step back.
solution.shortcut: wish + had (now); wish + had had / had done (past).

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: The bank has rewarded the clerk whom, according to the customers, deserved the award most.
The candidate whom the panel selected has more than five years of banking experience.
The clerk who everyone believed would retire soon has applied for an extension.
Whom shall I contact if the cheque is not credited to my account by Monday?

steps: Sentence A is incorrect. The pronoun is the subject of 'deserved' (he deserved the award), so it must be 'who'. The phrase 'according to the customers' between the commas does not change its role.
Correct: *The bank has rewarded the clerk who, according to the customers, deserved the award most.*

The other three are correct: B 'whom' is the object of 'selected' (the panel selected him); C 'who' is the subject of 'would retire'; 'everyone believed' is only inserted; D 'whom' is the object of 'contact' (I shall contact whom?).
solution.rule: Pronoun case: who (subject of its own verb) vs whom (object)
solution.trap: Sentence C has an inserted phrase too ('everyone believed') and correctly keeps 'who'. Remove the inserted words and test each case with he/him.
solution.shortcut: Answer with he → who; with him → whom.

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: Fewer people visited the fair this year because of the heavy rain.
The amount of paperwork needed for a home loan has come down considerably this year.
There have been less withdrawals from the ATM since the branch began opening its cash counter on Saturdays.
A little care can prevent most of the accidents that happen on the factory floor.

steps: Sentence C is incorrect. 'Withdrawals' is a countable plural, so it needs 'fewer', not 'less': 'There have been fewer withdrawals'.
Correct: *There have been fewer withdrawals from the ATM since the branch began opening its cash counter on Saturdays.*
The other three are correct: A uses 'fewer' with the countable 'people'; B uses 'amount of' with the uncountable 'paperwork' and a singular verb; D uses 'a little' with the uncountable 'care'.
solution.rule: Countability: fewer + countable plural; less + uncountable
solution.trap: The long tail of the sentence draws attention to tense ('have been … since'), which is correct; the quantifier is the error.
solution.shortcut: Can you put a number before it (three withdrawals)? → fewer.

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: Not only did the bank waive the penalty, but it also extended the repayment period.
Rarely do we see such long queues at the branch on a weekday.
Hardly had the guests sat down for dinner when the power went off.
Only after the documents were verified the loan was sanctioned by the manager.

steps: Sentence D is incorrect. A sentence that opens with 'Only after …' needs inversion in the main clause: 'Only after the documents were verified was the loan sanctioned by the manager.'
Correct: *Only after the documents were verified was the loan sanctioned by the manager.*
The other three are correct: A inverts after an opening 'Not only' and keeps normal order after 'but'; B inverts after the negative adverb 'rarely'; C inverts after 'hardly' and pairs it with 'when'.
solution.rule: Inversion: Only after / Only when / Only if + clause → auxiliary + subject in the main clause
solution.trap: The inversion goes in the main clause, not in the 'after' clause, so the sentence looks complete without it.
solution.shortcut: Opening 'Only + time phrase' → was / did / had + subject.

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: The principal, together with three teachers, has gone to Delhi for a workshop.
The cost of the repairs carried out on the three old ATMs were higher than expected.
The list of passengers who missed the flight was sent to the airline office.
Each of the employees has been asked to update the nominee details in the records.

steps: Sentence B is incorrect. The head noun of the subject is 'cost', which is singular; 'of the repairs carried out on the three old ATMs' only describes it. The verb must be 'was'.
Correct: *The cost of the repairs carried out on the three old ATMs was higher than expected.*
The other three are correct: A 'together with three teachers' does not change the singular subject → 'has'; C the head noun 'list' is singular → 'was'; D 'each of' takes a singular verb.
solution.rule: Subject–verb agreement: the verb agrees with the head noun, not with a noun inside an 'of' phrase
solution.trap: Two plural nouns ('repairs', 'ATMs') stand between the subject and the verb and pull you towards 'were'.
solution.shortcut: Strip the phrase: 'The cost … was'.

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: The new clerk is capable to handle the cash counter without any supervision.
The manager made the trainee rewrite the report because it had several errors.
Instead of waiting for the bus, we decided to walk to the station.
Having worked in audit for years, she is used to working late at the end of the financial year.

steps: Sentence A is incorrect. 'Capable' takes 'of' + gerund, not a to-infinitive: 'capable of handling the cash counter'. (Its synonym 'able' is the one that takes 'to'.)
Correct: *The new clerk is capable of handling the cash counter without any supervision.*

The other three are correct: B 'make' + object + bare infinitive in the active voice; C a gerund after 'instead of', a to-infinitive after 'decided'; D 'be used to' + gerund, with a correctly attached participle phrase.
solution.rule: Verb form: capable of + -ing; able to + base verb
solution.trap: 'able to handle' is correct, and the meanings are the same, so 'capable to handle' sounds right.
solution.shortcut: capable of doing / able to do.

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: The new branch is twice as large as the old one but has the same number of staff.
Of all the other branches in the region, ours has recorded the highest growth in deposits this year.
Of the two proposals, the second is more practical and less expensive.
This year's results are far better than those of the previous year.

steps: Sentence B is incorrect. With a superlative, the group must include the thing being compared. 'Our' branch cannot be one of 'all the other branches', so 'other' must go: 'Of all the branches in the region, ours …'.
Correct: *Of all the branches in the region, ours has recorded the highest growth in deposits this year.*
The other three are correct: A 'twice as … as' is the correct pattern for multiples; C uses comparatives for a choice between two; D compares results with results ('those of'), like with like.
solution.rule: Comparison: comparative + 'any other'; superlative + 'of all' (without 'other')
solution.trap: 'any other' is correct with a comparative ('higher than any other branch'), and that pattern is wrongly carried over to the superlative.
solution.shortcut: -er than any other; -est of all.

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: No sooner had the results been announced than the bank's website crashed under the load.
Unless the bill is paid today, the connection will be cut off tomorrow.
Leave early lest you should miss the last bus to the village.
She neither called the bank nor she visited the branch to report the lost card.

steps: Sentence D is incorrect. Correlatives must join matching parts. 'neither' stands before the verb 'called', so 'nor' must also be followed by a verb: 'She neither called the bank nor visited the branch'. The repeated 'she' breaks the parallel.
Correct: *She neither called the bank nor visited the branch to report the lost card.*
The other three are correct: A pairs 'no sooner' with 'than' and inverts after it; B uses 'unless' without an extra 'not'; C uses 'lest … should' + base verb.
solution.rule: Correlative conjunctions: neither … nor / either … or / not only … but also join parallel elements
solution.trap: 'neither … nor' is the right pair here, so the sentence looks correct; check what comes after each word.
solution.shortcut: Same type of word after both halves: verb … verb.

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: Everyone in the office except she had submitted the leave form before the deadline.
The two sisters helped each other with the household chores during the festival.
Each of the girls has brought her own lunch box to the picnic.
We availed ourselves of the special discount offered to senior citizens at the pharmacy.

steps: Sentence A is incorrect. 'Except' is a preposition, so the pronoun after it takes the object form: 'except her'.
Correct: *Everyone in the office except her had submitted the leave form before the deadline.*
The other three are correct: B uses 'each other' for two people; C 'each' takes a singular verb and the singular pronoun 'her'; D 'avail' takes a reflexive object + 'of'.
solution.rule: Pronoun case: object form after prepositions (except, between, for, with)
solution.trap: 'she' seems to belong with 'had submitted', but the subject of that verb is 'everyone'; 'except her' is only a prepositional phrase.
solution.shortcut: Drop 'Everyone in the office': 'except she' alone is clearly wrong.

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: My uncle retired from the railways in 2019 and now runs a small grocery shop.
The guests have been waiting in the lobby for over an hour.
Sushma has completed her graduation in commerce from Delhi University in 2021.
We have never seen such a large crowd at the village fair before.

steps: Sentence C is incorrect. 'in 2021' is a definite past time, and the present perfect cannot be used with it. It should be 'Sushma completed her graduation …'.
Correct: *Sushma completed her graduation in commerce from Delhi University in 2021.*

The other three are correct: A the simple past with '2019' and the simple present with 'now'; B the present perfect continuous with 'for' + a period up to now; D the present perfect with 'never … before', which has no fixed time.
solution.rule: Tense: simple past with a stated past time (in 2021, last year, ago)
solution.trap: The result still matters today (she is a graduate), which makes the present perfect tempting; the dated time phrase rules it out.
solution.shortcut: Year / date / ago in the sentence → simple past.

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: There are many reasons why young people prefer digital payments to cash.
On the notice board was pasted the names of the candidates selected for the interview.
Here comes the bus that goes directly to the airport without stopping anywhere.
Behind the old bank building stand two huge banyan trees planted by its founder.

steps: Sentence B is incorrect. The sentence is inverted; the real subject 'the names' comes after the verb and is plural, so the verb must be 'were pasted'.
Correct: *On the notice board were pasted the names of the candidates selected for the interview.*

The other three are correct: A 'there are' agrees with the plural 'reasons'; 'prefer … to'; C in the inverted sentence the singular subject 'the bus' takes 'comes'; D in the inverted sentence the plural subject 'trees' takes 'stand'.
solution.rule: Subject–verb agreement in inverted sentences: the verb agrees with the subject that follows
solution.trap: The singular 'notice board' stands before the verb and looks like the subject.
solution.shortcut: Rewrite in normal order: 'The names … were pasted on the notice board'.

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: The bank has decided to dispense with the old system of manual registers.
The court acquitted the driver of all the charges brought against him.
The scheme is meant to provide relief to farmers affected by the drought.
The manager was angry on the clerk for coming late to the branch again.

steps: Sentence D is incorrect. 'Angry' takes 'with' before a person (and 'at' or 'about' before a thing): 'angry with the clerk'.
Correct: *The manager was angry with the clerk for coming late to the branch again.*
The other three are correct: A 'dispense with' = do without; B 'acquit someone of' a charge; C 'provide relief to' someone.
solution.rule: Prepositions: angry with (a person), angry at / about (a thing)
solution.trap: 'angry on' is a direct translation from Hindi ('us par gussa'), so it feels natural to many readers.

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: While waiting for the bus, a stray dog started barking at the children.
The new manager is known for his honesty, his patience and his punctuality.
Walking along the platform, I saw an old friend I had not met in years.
Having finished the audit, the officers left the branch late in the evening.

steps: Sentence A is incorrect. The opening phrase 'While waiting for the bus' has no subject of its own, so it attaches to the subject of the main clause, 'a stray dog'. It was the children who were waiting, so the modifier dangles.
Correct: *While the children were waiting for the bus, a stray dog started barking at them.*

The other three are correct: B the three items in the list are parallel nouns; C the subject 'I' is the one walking, so the phrase is attached correctly; D the subject 'the officers' finished the audit.
solution.rule: Modifiers: an opening participle phrase must refer to the subject of the main clause
solution.trap: Sentences C and D have the same structure but are correct, because their subjects ('I', 'the officers') really do the action in the opening phrase.
solution.shortcut: Ask 'who was waiting?' — the answer must be the subject after the comma.

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: The furniture in the new office was bought from a shop in Jodhpur.
The restaurant owner replaced all the broken crockeries in the kitchen after the festival rush.
Mathematics is the subject that most students in our class find difficult.
The people of this village depend mainly on fishing for their livelihood.

steps: Sentence B is incorrect. 'Crockery' (cups, plates and dishes as a group) is uncountable and has no plural: 'all the broken crockery'.
Correct: *The restaurant owner replaced all the broken crockery in the kitchen after the festival rush.*
The other three are correct: A 'furniture' is uncountable and takes 'was'; C 'mathematics' is singular despite the -s; D 'people' is plural and takes 'depend'.
solution.rule: Countability: 'crockery' is uncountable
solution.trap: Sentences A and C test countability too, and they look suspicious ('furniture … was', 'Mathematics is') but are correct.
solution.shortcut: crockery, cutlery, furniture, jewellery → no -s.

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: Sunita is one of those employees who never take a day off without informing the manager.
Arun is the only one of the clerks who knows how to operate the new cash machine.
Each of the branch heads, along with two officers, were invited to the annual meeting at the head office.
A number of complaints regarding the new app have reached the head office.

steps: Sentence C is incorrect. The subject is 'each' (singular). Neither 'of the branch heads' nor 'along with two officers' changes that, so the verb must be 'was invited'.
Correct: *Each of the branch heads, along with two officers, was invited to the annual meeting at the head office.*
The other three are correct: A 'who' refers to 'those employees' (plural) → 'take'; B 'who' refers to 'the only one' (singular) → 'knows'; D 'a number of' (= many) takes a plural verb.
solution.rule: Subject–verb agreement: 'each of' + an 'along with' phrase → still singular
solution.trap: Two plural nouns ('heads', 'officers') sit before the verb. Sentences A and B look like a mismatched pair ('take' vs 'knows'), but both are correct.
solution.shortcut: Find the true subject: each → was.

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: Had the bank checked the signature carefully, the fraud would not have happened.
If I had taken the job in Chennai last year, I would be living near the sea now.
Were the bank to reduce its interest rate, more people would apply for home loans.
Should the customer will need any help, the clerk at the enquiry counter will assist him.

steps: Sentence D is incorrect. In an inverted first conditional, 'Should' replaces 'if' and is followed by the base verb: 'Should the customer need any help'. 'will' cannot follow 'should'.
Correct: *Should the customer need any help, the clerk at the enquiry counter will assist him.*

The other three are correct: A inverted third conditional: Had + subject + V3, would have + V3; B mixed conditional: past condition, present result; C inverted second conditional: Were + subject + to-infinitive.
solution.rule: Conditionals: Should + subject + base verb (= If + subject + present)
solution.trap: All four sentences are conditionals and three are inverted, so they all look unusual. Only one has two modals in a row.
solution.shortcut: Should / Had / Were at the start = 'if'; check the verb form after each.

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: This is the first time I am visiting the branch at Panaji, so I need directions.
It was the first time that the bank had held its annual meeting outside Mumbai.
It is the second time this month that the ATM has run out of cash.
Since he joined the bank in 2018, Prakash has been promoted twice.

steps: Sentence A is incorrect. After 'This / It is the first (second …) time', the present perfect is used: 'This is the first time I have visited the branch at Panaji'.
Correct: *This is the first time I have visited the branch at Panaji, so I need directions.*
The other three are correct: B 'It was the first time' + past perfect; C 'It is the second time' + present perfect; D the simple past in the 'since' clause and the present perfect in the main clause.
solution.rule: Tense: It is the first time + present perfect; It was the first time + past perfect
solution.trap: The visit is happening now, so the present continuous feels natural; this fixed pattern needs the perfect tense.
solution.shortcut: is the first time → have + V3; was the first time → had + V3.

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: The secretary and the treasurer of the cooperative society have both resigned this week.
None of the money that was collected for the flood victims were deposited in the bank.
Each of the four branches in the district has its own locker facility.
Physics, as well as chemistry, is taught by the same teacher in our school.

steps: Sentence B is incorrect. 'None of' + an uncountable noun ('the money') takes a singular verb: 'was deposited'. The relative clause correctly uses 'was collected', and the main verb must match.
Correct: *None of the money that was collected for the flood victims was deposited in the bank.*

The other three are correct: A two people ('the' repeated) → plural verb; C 'each of' → singular verb and singular 'its'; D the verb agrees with 'Physics' (singular); the 'as well as' phrase is ignored.
solution.rule: Subject–verb agreement: none / all / some / any of + uncountable noun → singular verb
solution.trap: 'flood victims' (plural) stands right before the verb. With a plural noun ('none of the victims'), either verb form can be accepted, but with 'money' only the singular is possible.
solution.shortcut: none of the money → was; none of the files → was / were.

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: The farmers have been demanding that the canal be cleaned before the sowing season.
The old bridge, which had been closed for repairs, was finally reopened last week.
The bank has risen its interest rates on fixed deposits twice this year.
The thief was caught red-handed while trying to break open the locker.

steps: Sentence C is incorrect. 'Rise – rose – risen' is intransitive and cannot take an object. To increase something, use the transitive 'raise – raised – raised': 'The bank has raised its interest rates'.
Correct: *The bank has raised its interest rates on fixed deposits twice this year.*

The other three are correct: A subjunctive 'be cleaned' after 'demanding that'; B past perfect passive for the earlier state, simple past for 'last week'; D the idiom 'caught red-handed' and 'break open' are used correctly.
solution.rule: Verb form: rise (intransitive: rates rise) vs raise (transitive: the bank raises rates)
solution.trap: 'has risen' is a correct form of 'rise' ('Rates have risen'), so it looks fine; it cannot take the object 'its interest rates'. Sentence A's 'be cleaned' is also correct, not an agreement error.
solution.shortcut: Object after it? → raise / raised.

items.prompt: Which of the following sentences is grammatically incorrect? If all the sentences are correct, choose 'All are correct'.
options: Scarcely had the auditors left when the manager called an emergency meeting.
Not until the payment was confirmed did the shop release the goods.
The number of women opening savings accounts in villages has risen steadily.
Hardly any of the money that was raised has been spent so far.

steps: All four sentences are correct. Each one has a pattern that looks wrong but follows the rule.

A: 'scarcely' + inversion + 'when'; B: 'Not until …' + inversion in the main clause (did + subject + base verb); C: 'the number of' → singular verb; intransitive 'risen' with no object; D: 'any of' + uncountable 'money' → singular 'has'; transitive 'raised' for money collected.
solution.rule: No error: inversion after scarcely / not until; 'the number of'; 'any of + uncountable'; rise vs raise
solution.trap: Every sentence has something that looks suspicious (inversions, 'has risen' next to 'raised'). Mark a sentence only if you can name the rule it breaks.
solution.shortcut: Check each sentence against one rule; four passes → 'All are correct'.
